After exploring 12 articles, the research team examined the different problems Food at Home addresses, including food waste and money waste, shared household conflicts over shared resources, and motivation for building habits.
Identifying common and recurring themes helped us define our problem statement and focus. We learned it is important to define our scope early so we do not run out of steam.

This research validated our target audience and made it more specific. Our primary audience is young adults ages 23-34 who recently graduated and moved out with unrelated roommates. Our secondary audience is people ages 18-22 who moved out at a younger age. They are likely to grocery shop occasionally, but not as regularly or frequently as the primary audience.

Although we know people who cook regularly, they do not represent most people in this age range, who cook only as needed. The new age range helped us understand users’ financial constraints and their likelihood of living with a roommate.
We researched potential ways to convert our codebase into a mobile app, as well as other pathways for mobile app implementation.

Our team chose React Native with Expo and TestFlight because it gave us the ability to create a unified codebase for both iOS and Android, if we had enough time to implement both, which would increase our user base. We decided against other methods, like building a PWA, because they would have been too complicated, especially on iOS.
The summary compiled all of the key data collected from the 12 articles into one condensed document.

Creating the summary reduced the time needed to search for relevant data. It defined our scope and gave us a clearer direction. It also identified the strongest research points and the topics that needed more support.
This persona encapsulated key characteristics from our target demographic and highlighted goals and pain points to help us understand the user’s journey.

This collaborative session allowed us to brain dump every team member’s thoughts without dismissing any ideas. We narrowed our work down to three core features and established a strong foundation for our critical flows.

We reviewed the existing prototype and documented the current app structure, including its main screens, features, and navigation hierarchy. This map served as a reference for identifying structural improvements and developing the proposed app map.

We established a clear overview of the existing app structure, which helped the team understand how features were organized and identify opportunities to improve navigation and accommodate new features.

Using data about our target audience and the pain points we researched in our preliminary book research, we reused our persona, Aiden, and mapped his experience from identifying his frustration, to attempting to address the issue, to acquiring the app, testing the service, and finally becoming loyal to it.

The journey map once again helped us empathize with users and understand their pain points, how they might address their issues, and where our app could offer help. The journey map informed our user flow.

Each researcher sat in on at least one 30-minute interview. Roles were split into moderator and notetaker, with notetakers taking notes through a Qualtrics form.

title: Research AI Parsing in Receipt Scans

children.text: Intensive research was done to find receipt parsing related APIs and tools to integrate within our application, so that users can have their receipts accurately read.
The most optimal tool for receipt parsing integration would be Anthropic API (Claude), with the version being Sonnet 5.5 due to speed and accuracy.
The research team created a quick color preference survey for our 4 new proposed palettes. The survey mimics that of a desirability survey.

There was a discussion between utilizing an ABCD testing format and a desirability survey. We decided to implement aspects of both in our preference test. We had established our adjectives in a brand brief conducted at the beginning of the quarter, but this survey will further validate our words and open up consideration to other directions we can go in for colors.
Team Cronch created a project timeline to evaluate our progress and estimate the timeframe for Winter Quarter.
This timeline ensured that our goals for next term are properly laid out. We laid out milestones, tasks, and even dates for holidays to make sure we stay on top of our work.

In order to consolidate specific colors on our UI, each designer separately created a palette with colors that would complement our brand. Color Exploration included colors centered around green, purple, peach, orange, and pink. The individual palettes were blind tested and adjusted after voting to see which colors matched each other the best visually. They were then consolidated into 4 distinct palettes.

Many designers had similar visions, and it was interesting to see how they were all executed. It took a lot of adjusting to see which colors were suited for each other, and which would stand out more on the screen.

After the color palettes were finalized with 4 distinct directions, the assets were compiled into PNGs to send to the research team for testing. Along with the color palettes, two assets were created to test out the placement of the “+” on the menu bar.

Preparing the assets for preference testing helped us compare different visual directions consistently. By keeping the layout and content the same, we can focus on how users respond to the color palettes.
The low fidelity screens of our critical path were coded out and launched on to Testflight. Users are able to add items to inventory via receipt scan.
Having the critical path ready for further development in the next term puts us at a good spot in our progress.
